source_text: Ἔξεστι δὲ ἡμῖν ἐκ περιουσίας πρὸς τοὺς φιλεγκλήμονας ἐπαποδύσασθαι· οὐ γὰρ παῖδες ἡμεῖς καὶ νήπιοι πρὸς τὸ παιδαριῶδες καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητον τῆς μαθήσεως προσηγορεύμεθα, καθὼς οἱ εἰς γνῶσιν πεφυσιωμένοι διαβεβλήκασιν· ἀναγεννηθέντες γοῦν εὐθέως τὸ τέλειον ἀπειλήφαμεν, οὗ ἕνεκεν ἐσπεύδομεν. ἐφωτίσθημεν γάρ· τὸ δὲ ἔστιν ἐπιγνῶναι τὸν θεόν. οὔκουν ἀτελὴς ὁ ἐγνωκὼς τὸ τέλειον. καί μου μὴ λάβησθε ὁμολογοῦντος ἐγνωκέναι τὸν θεόν. ὧδέ πως γὰρ ἔδοξεν εἰπεῖν τῷ λόγῳ· ὃ δὲ ἐλεύθερος. αὐτίκα γοῦν βαπτιζομένῳ τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπ᾿ οὐρανῶν ἐπήχησε φωνὴ μάρτυς ἠγαπημένου »υἱός μου εἶ σὺ ἀγαπητός, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε.« πυθώμεθα οὖν τῶν σοφῶν· σήμερον ἀναγεννηθεὶς ὁ Χριστὸς ἤδη τέλειός ἐστιν ἤ, ὅπερ ἀτοπώτατον, ἐλλιπής. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, προσμαθεῖν τι αὐτῷ δεῖ. ἀλλὰ προσμαθεῖν μὲν αὐτὸν εἰκὸς οὐδὲ ἓν θεὸν ὄντα. οὐ γὰρ ἂν μείζων τις εἴη τοῦ λόγου οὐδὲ μὴν διδάσκαλος τοῦ μόνου διδασκάλου. μή τι οὖν ὁμολογήσουσιν ἄκοντες τὸν λόγον, τέλειον ἐκ τελείου φύντα τοῦ πατρός, κατὰ τὴν οἰκονομικὴν προδιατύπωσιν ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείως; καὶ εἰ τέλειος ἦν, τί ἐβαπτίζετο ὁ τέλειος; ἔδει, φασί, πληρῶσαι τὸ ἐπάγγελμα τὸ ἀνθρώπινον. παγκάλως. φημὶ γάρ· ἅμα τοίνυν τῷ βαπτίζεσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ Ἰωάννου γίνεται τέλειος; δῆλον ὅτι. οὐδὲν οὖν πρὸς αὐτοῦ προσέμαθεν; οὐ γάρ. τελειοῦται δὲ τῷ λουτρῷ μόνῳ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος τῇ καθόδῳ ἁγιάζεται; οὕτως ἔχει. Τὸ δὲ αὐτὸ συμβαίνει τοῦτο καὶ περὶ ἡμᾶς, ὧν γέγονεν ὑπογραφὴ ὁ κύριος· βαπτιζόμενοι φωτιζόμεθα, φωτιζόμενοι υἱοποιούμεθα, υἱοποιούμενοι τελειούμεθα, τελειούμενοι ἀπαθανατιζόμεθα »ἐγώ«, φησίν, »εἶπα, θεοί ἐστε καὶ υἱοὶ ὑψίστου πάντες.« καλεῖται δὲ πολλαχῶς τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο, χάρισμα καὶ φώτισμα καὶ τέλειον καὶ λουτρόν· λουτρὸν μὲν δι᾿ οὗ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἀπορρυπτόμεθα, χάρισμα δὲ ᾧ τὰ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν ἐπιτίμια ἀνεῖται, φώτισμα δὲ δι᾿ οὗ τὸ ἅγιον ἐκεῖνο φῶς τὸ σωτήριον ἐποπτεύεται, τουτέστιν δι᾿ οὗ τὸ θεῖον ὀξυωποῦμεν, τέλειον δὲ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς φαμέν. τί γὰρ ἔτι λείπεται τῷ θεὸν ἐγνωκότι; καὶ γὰρ ἄτοπον ὡς ἀληθῶς χάρισμα κεκλῆσθαι θεοῦ τὸ μὴ πεπληρωμένον· τέλειος δὲ ὢν τέλεια χαριεῖται δήπουθεν· ὡς δὲ ἅμα τῷ κελεῦσαι αὐτὸν πάντα γίνεται, οὕτως ἕπεται τῷ χαρίσασθαι μόνον βουληθῆναι αὐτὸν τὸ πεπληρῶσθαι τὴν χάριν. τὸ γὰρ μέλλον τοῦ χρόνου τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ θελήματος προλαμβάνεται. πρὸς δὲ καὶ ἡ τῶν κακῶν ἀπαλλαγὴ σωτηρίας ἐστὶν ἀρχή. μόνον δὲ ἄρα οἱ πρῶτον δραξάμενοι τῶν ὅρων τῆς ζωῆς ἤδη τέλειοι, ζῶμεν δὲ ἤδη οἱ θανάτου κεχωρισμένοι. σωτηρία τοίνυν τὸ ἕπεσθαι Χριστῷ. »ὃ γὰρ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ, ζωή ἐστιν.« »ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν,« φησίν, »ὁ τὸν λόγον μου ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων τῷ πέμψαντί με ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον καὶ εἰς κρίσιν οὐκ ἔρχεται, ἀλλὰ μεταβέβηκεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωήν.« οὕτω τὸ πιστεῦσαι μόνον καὶ ἀναγεννηθῆναι τελείωσίς ἐστιν ἐν ζωῇ· οὐ γάρ ποτε ἀσθενεῖ ὁ θεός. ὡς γὰρ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ ἔργον ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦτο κόσμος ὀνομάζεται, οὕτως καὶ τὸ βούλημα αὐτοῦ ἀνθρώπων ἐστὶ σωτηρία καὶ τοῦτο ἐκκλησία κέκληται. οἶδεν οὖν οὓς κέκληκεν, οὓς δὲ κέκληκεν, σέσωκεν· κέκληκεν δὲ ἅμα καὶ σέσωκεν. »αὐτοὶ γὰρ ὑμεῖς«, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος, »θεοδίδακτοί ἐστε.« οὐκ ἄρα θεμιτὸν ἡμῖν ἀτελὲς τὸ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ διδασκόμενον νοεῖν, τὸ δὲ μάθημα ἀίδιος σωτηρία ἀιδίου σωτῆρος, ᾧ ἡ χάρις εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, ἀμήν. καὶ ὁ μόνον ἀναγεννηθείς, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ τοὔνομα ἔχει, φωτισθεὶς ἀπήλλακται μὲν παραχρῆμα τοῦ σκότους, ἀπείληφεν δὲ αὐτόθεν τὸ φῶς. ὥσπερ οὖν οἱ τὸν ὕπνον ἀποσεισάμενοι εὐθέως ἔνδοθεν ἐγρηγόρασιν, μᾶλλον δὲ καθάπερ οἱ τὸ ὑπόχυμα τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν κατάγειν πειρώμενοι οὐ τὸ φῶς αὑτοῖς ἔξωθεν χορηγοῦσιν, ὃ οὐκ ἔχουσιν, τὸ δὲ ἐμπόδιον ταῖς ὄψεσι καταβιβάζοντες ἐλευθέραν ἀπολείπουσι τὴν κόρην, οὕτως καὶ οἱ βαπτιζόμενοι, τὰς ἐπισκοτούσας ἁμαρτίας τῷ θείῳ πνεύματι ἀχλύος δίκην ἀποτριψάμενοι, ἐλεύθερον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον καὶ φωτεινὸν ὄμμα τοῦ πνεύματος ἴσχομεν, ᾧ δὴ μόνῳ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύομεν, οὐρανόθεν ἐπεισρέοντος ἡμῖν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος· κρᾶμα τοῦτο αὐγῆς ἀιδίου τὸ ἀίδιον φῶς ἰδεῖν δυναμένης· ἐπεὶ τὸ ὅμοιον τῷ ὁμοίῳ φίλον, φίλον δὲ τὸ ἅγιον τῷ ἐξ οὗ τὸ ἅγιον, ὃ δὴ κυρίως κέκληται φῶς· »ἦτε γάρ ποτε σκότος, νῦν δὲ φῶς ἐν κυρίῳ.« ἐντεῦθεν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ὑπὸ τῶν παλαιῶν ἡγοῦμαι κεκλῆσθαι φῶτα.
pass_a_gloss: It is possible for us to divest ourselves of superfluity towards those who are fond of niceties; for we are not children and infants in relation to the childish and easily despised learning, as those who have been puffed up towards knowledge have slandered; for having been reborn, we immediately received the perfect, on account of which we are hastening. For we have been enlightened; and this is to know God. Therefore, the one who has known the perfect is not imperfect. And do not take hold of me as confessing that I have known God. For thus it seemed right to the Word to say; but what is free. Immediately, therefore, when the Lord was being baptized from heaven, a voice sounded as a witness, 'You are my beloved Son, today I have begotten you.' Let us ask, then, the wise; today, having been reborn, is Christ already perfect or, which is absurd, imperfect? But if this is the case, it is necessary for him to learn something. But it is not likely that he, being God, would need to learn even one thing. For no one would be greater than the Word, nor even a teacher of the only Teacher. Will they not, therefore, confess against their will that the Word, having been born perfect from the perfect Father, according to the economic pre-arrangement, was reborn perfectly? And if he was perfect, why was the perfect one baptized? It was necessary, they say, to fulfill the human promise. Beautifully, I say; for when he was being baptized by John, did he become perfect immediately? It is clear that he did. Therefore, did he not learn anything in addition to this? No, he did not. For he is perfected by the bath alone, and he is sanctified by the descent of the Spirit; this is how it is. The same thing happens to us, of whom the Lord has become a guarantee; when we are baptized, we are enlightened, when we are enlightened, we are made sons, when we are made sons, we are perfected, when we are perfected, we are made immortal. 'For I have said,' he says, 'you are gods and all sons of the Most High.' And this work is called by many names: a gift and enlightenment and perfection and bath; a bath, indeed, through which we wash away our sins; a gift, by which the penalties for our sins are remitted; enlightenment, through which that holy and salvific light is beheld; that is, through which we perceive the divine. Perfection, we say, is what is without need; for what is still lacking to the one who has known God? And it is also absurd, indeed, for the gift of God to be called imperfect; but the perfect one, being perfect, gives perfect gifts; just as everything comes into being when he commands, so also it follows that when he gives, he wills only that the gift be fulfilled. For the future is anticipated by the power of his will. And the removal of evils is the beginning of salvation. Only those, therefore, who have first grasped the boundaries of life are already perfect; and we, having been separated from death, are already living. Therefore, salvation is to follow Christ; 'for what has come into being in him is life.' 'Amen, amen, I say to you,' he says, 'the one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.' Thus, to believe and to be reborn is perfection in life; for God is not weak at any time. Just as his will is a work, and this is called the world, so also the will of God is the salvation of humans, and this is called the church. He knows, therefore, those whom he has called, and those whom he has called, he has saved; and he has called and saved them at the same time. 'For you are taught by God,' the apostle says. It is not lawful, therefore, for us to consider the teaching under him as imperfect, but the lesson is eternal salvation from the eternal Savior, to whom be the glory forever, amen. And the one who has been reborn alone, as the name also has it, having been enlightened, has immediately been freed from darkness and has received the light from that moment. Just as those who have shaken off sleep are immediately awake from within, or rather, just as those who try to remove the rheum from their eyes do not provide the light for themselves from outside, which they do not have, but by removing the obstacle from their sight, they leave the pupil free, so also those who are baptized, having wiped away the sins that overshadowed them like a cloud by the divine Spirit, possess a free and unobstructed and shining eye of the spirit, by which alone we behold the divine, with the Holy Spirit pouring in from heaven; this is the mixture of eternal light, which is able to see the eternal light; since what is like is friendly to what is like, and the holy is friendly to the one from whom the holy comes, which is properly called light; 'for you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.' From this, I consider that man has been called light by the ancients.

choices.why: The Greek verb ἐπαποδύω means to divest oneself of something, in this case, superfluity.
The Greek verb τελειόω means to perfect or to make complete.
The Greek word χάρισμα refers to a gift or a favor, in this case, the gift of salvation.
The Greek verb ἐποπτεύω means to behold or to gaze at something, in this case, the divine.
The Greek word ἐκκλησία refers to a gathering or assembly of people, in this case, the church.

bible_refs.note: The voice from heaven says, 'You are my beloved Son, today I have begotten you.'
Jesus says, 'Amen, amen, I say to you, the one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.'

pass_b_english: We are permitted to strip away all superfluity when we address those who are fond of niceties, for we are neither children nor infants when it comes to that childish and easily despised learning, despite how those puffed up with knowledge have slandered us. Having been reborn, we immediately received the perfect reality toward which we were hastening; for we have been enlightened, and enlightenment is nothing other than knowing God. Consequently, the one who has known the perfect is not imperfect. Do not, however, seize on my words as if I were confessing that I have known God fully. The Word saw fit to put it this way: 'What is free.' At the very moment the Lord was being baptized, a voice from heaven sounded as a witness: 'You are my beloved Son; today I have begotten you' (Luke 3:22). Let us then ask the wise: today, having been reborn, is Christ already perfect, or, which is absurd, imperfect? If the latter, he would need to learn something. Yet it is not plausible that he, being God, would need to learn even a single thing. No one is greater than the Word, nor could anyone serve as a teacher of the only Teacher. Will they not therefore confess against their will that the Word, born perfect from the perfect Father, was reborn perfectly in accordance with the economy's pre-arrangement? And if he was perfect, why was the perfect one baptized? 'It was necessary,' they say, 'to fulfill the human promise.' Beautifully said, I reply; for at the very moment he was being baptized by John, did he become perfect? Clearly he did. Therefore, did he learn nothing in addition? No, he did not. He is perfected by the bath alone, and he is sanctified by the descent of the Spirit; that is how it stands. The same thing happens to us, for whom the Lord has become a guarantee: when we are baptized we are enlightened; when we are enlightened we are made sons; when we are made sons we are perfected; when we are perfected we are made immortal. 'I have said, "You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High"' (Ps 82:6). This work is called by many names: a gift, enlightenment, perfection, a bath. It is a bath because through it we wash away our sins; a gift because by it the penalties due for our sins are remitted; enlightenment because through it that holy and salvific light is beheld—that is, through it we perceive the divine. Perfection, we say, is what lacks nothing, for what is still lacking to the one who has known God? It is also absurd for the gift of God to be called imperfect; the perfect one, being perfect, gives perfect gifts. Just as everything comes into being when he commands, so it follows that when he gives, he wills only that the gift be fulfilled; the future is anticipated by the power of his will. Even the removal of evils is the beginning of salvation. Only those who have first grasped the boundaries of life are already perfect, and we who have been separated from death are already living. Salvation, therefore, is to follow Christ: 'For what has come into being in him is life' (John 1:4). 'Amen, amen, I say to you,' he says, 'the one who hears my word and believes in the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life' (John 5:24). Thus, to believe and to be reborn is perfection in life; for God is never weak. Just as his will is a work, and this is called the world, so the will of God is the salvation of humans, and this is called the church. He knows those whom he has called, and those whom he has called, he has saved; he called and saved them at the same time. 'For you yourselves are taught by God,' the apostle says (1 Thess 4:9). It is therefore not permissible for us to consider the teaching under him as imperfect; the lesson is eternal salvation from the eternal Savior, to whom be glory forever, amen. The one who has been reborn alone, as the very name implies, has been enlightened and immediately freed from darkness, receiving the light from that very moment. Just as those who shake off sleep are immediately awake from within, or rather, just as those who try to remove the rheum from their eyes do not supply light from outside—for they do not possess it—but by removing the obstacle from their sight leave the pupil free, so also those who are baptized, having wiped away the sins that overshadowed them like a cloud by the divine Spirit, possess a free, unobstructed, and shining eye of the spirit. By that eye alone we behold the divine, with the Holy Spirit pouring in from heaven; this mixture of eternal light is able to see the eternal light, since like is friendly to like, and the holy is friendly to the one from whom the holy comes, which is properly called light: 'For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord' (Eph 5:8). From this I consider that man has been called light by the ancients.
notes: The translation aims to convey the full scope of the passage, including the discussion of the 'work called by many names' and the detailed explanation of how the Spirit's descent sanctifies.
